conclusions: The reported 25-years-to-life range is legally plausible under §12.42(d), but the current corpus does not yet prove which two prior felony convictions the State alleged or whether their sequence satisfies the statute.
The best-supported current sentence fact is a 50-year jury-assessed TDCJ term as stated in the agency-authored release; the signed judgment remains a higher-priority missing native record.

A 50-year sentence does not itself prove a 25-year parole date or any release date. Parole eligibility and release must remain unresolved until the judgment/offense classification and TDCJ calculation are recovered.
Secondary reporting that an appeal was filed remains a lead, not a native appellate-docket fact.
counterarguments: The DA release is a prosecution-authored account and is not independent proof of the indictment, prior judgments, self-representation waiver or punishment election.
A fifth DWI count alone does not establish the habitual-felony enhancement; §12.42(d) requires separate qualifying final felony predicates with the statutory sequence.
findings: The Montgomery County DA's official index lists `State of Texas vs. Eugenio Les Zavala` dated July 23, 2026.
The agency-authored release says a jury in the 221st District Court convicted Zavala of Driving While Intoxicated (Third or More) after a July 20–21, 2026 trial and assessed 50 years in TDCJ.

The same prosecution account says the stop produced a warrant-obtained blood result of 0.150 after Zavala declined field sobriety testing and requested breath/blood specimens, and says he represented himself with standby counsel.
Texas Penal Code §49.09(b)(2) independently establishes that two qualifying prior intoxication-operation convictions can elevate a current DWI to a third-degree felony.
Texas Penal Code §12.42(d) independently establishes the 25–99 years or life habitual-felony range when two qualifying final felonies satisfy the sequential-finality rule.

Texas Code of Criminal Procedure art. 37.07 independently establishes that jury punishment requires the applicable statutory election/procedure; the fact that a jury tried guilt does not alone prove the punishment election.
